description:
We are Orbit To Field, a multidisciplinary team of six students: 3 mechanical engineers, 1 electrical engineer, 1 agricultural engineer, and 1 data analyst from EMI, IAV, and 1337.

Our mission is to leverage NASA satellite data to help farmers adapt to climate change through smarter, sustainable agricultural decisions.

Combining engineering, agriculture, and data science, we value innovation, teamwork, and problem-solving.

Our vision: Turning data from space into solutions on Earth!
summary:
Orbit2Field is a web platform that turns NASA Earth data into a farm plan. A farmer places a field on the map; NASA POWER supplies its climate history since 1981 and NASA GIBS adds satellite context, combined with the field’s soil, water and crop details.

In six steps, the platform ranks crop rotations by salinity, pH, field capacity, botanical families and degree-days, with agroforestry options; computes each rotation’s water gap (FAO-56) and designs a priced irrigation system; builds a degree-day sowing and growth calendar; recommends and pairs a soil sensor box; and replays the worst years on record to test each rotation against drought, excess rain and frost.

Saved fields get a daily recap with irrigation timing, sowing and harvest windows and frost, heat and storm alerts. An AI advisor explains results in plain language, and a community space connects growers and advisers. The tool works in English, French and Arabic.

It answers the Field Shift challenge by putting satellite data to work at parcel scale. NASA data covers any point on Earth; our agronomic database starts with Moroccan crops and can extend to other regions. As drought and climate shifts threaten farming worldwide, choosing resilient rotations and irrigating precisely saves water and protects yields and food security.
details:
What it does and how it works

  1. Locate and describe: the farmer pins the parcel and enters crop history, soil lab values, water source, equipment and priorities (water saving, income, soil building, erosion, forage, nitrogen).
  2. Read the sky: NASA POWER daily data become field features: frost and heat days, rain, evaporation, root-zone wetness, water balance and trends.
  3. Rank rotations: an explainable, rule-based engine checks botanical family, thermal fit (degree-days), soil and pH compatibility, water stress and succession rules. It compares ≥3 strategies and shows evidence, risks and gaps.
  4. Stress-test: the Regret Map replays each rotation across 16 shifted climate futures. It shows which option you would regret least, not just which wins on average.
  5. Act: irrigation design (ETc = ET0 × Kc minus effective rain, hydraulic sizing, priced equipment), season calendar by growth stage, sensor-box matching (110 boxes), and a daily recap with recommended decisions that stays in the field’s history.
  6. Learn and share: observed growth stages recalibrate the model per field, and farmers exchange advice in community channels.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Less water wasted, fewer bare-soil months, better soil health and a more resilient income.
  • Agronomy that was out of reach for smallholders becomes free and local. The first target is Morocco (Souss, Tadla, Saïss, with 16 crops), and the design is portable to any region.
  • Impact goal: more farms that survive drought years, and a growing database of real field outcomes.

Tools and stack
Python (FastAPI, a pure-stdlib engine with 117 tests that match a legacy engine on 50+ golden cases), PostgreSQL on Neon (row-level security, pgvector, full-text), JavaScript front end (Leaflet, Chart.js), Vercel serverless, open LLMs through an OpenAI-compatible API. Interface in English, French and Arabic.

What is creative

  • Regret, not averages: farmers choose under uncertainty, so we rank by robustness.
  • One field, one loop: rotation → irrigation → sensors → daily follow-up, driven by the same NASA data.
  • Calibrates itself from the farmer’s observations.
  • Honest by design: every number is labelled measured, modelled or placeholder.

Factors we considered
Low connectivity and low technical literacy; local prices in MAD; salinity as a Moroccan reality; transparency over a black box; data privacy (row-level security); cost, since everything runs on free tiers.
